title: Looking back: the Japji
hookLine: thirty-eight pauris heard and understood, one by one

cards: A whole scripture, read slowly, line by line: sound first, meaning second. That was camp four. Day after day it walked through Guru Nanak's Japji, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib and the first bani of a Sikh morning.
Each day began with a line said aloud in Gurmukhi, tongue-twisters and all. Then came what it meant. Somewhere in the middle, it may have stopped feeling like homework.

teach.h: THE MOOL MANTAR AND AAD SACH.
teach.b: It began before the first pauri, with the Mool Mantar: Ik Onkar, Satnam, one Creator, whose name is truth, without fear, without hate, beyond time, never born, self-existent, known by the Guru's grace.
Then the salok: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and true forever. Then pauri one, and its first line, said aloud back in camp four: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar.
Thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there. The way through is hukam, walking in the order. Pauri two: everything comes by that order, and whoever understands it stops saying I, I.
Then the great runs. Suniai: by listening. Mannai: by trusting.
Asankh: countless prayers and countless fools, and Nanak calling himself too small to count them.

Then the realms, one after another, like a ladder: duty, knowledge, effort, grace, and at the top, the realm of truth, where the Formless dwells. Pauri thirty-eight, the mint: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar.
Let restraint be the furnace and patience the goldsmith, and there the Word is minted. And last, the salok that closes it: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat.
Air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother.
From thinking you can't get there, to seeing the whole world as your family: that's the arc of the Japji.
If you walked those days with it, you've earned a plain sentence: I read it.

teach.h: THE MINT, AND AIR, WATER, EARTH.

teach.b: Read, one pauri at a time.

how: Many Sikhs recite the Japji every morning as the first of the daily banis, from memory or from a gutka, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib itself.

games.q: pauri one: you want to reach the truth, so you think about it a hundred thousand times. what does the Japji say?
o: thinking won't reach it; walk in the order, hukam.
games.why: sochai soch na hovaee: thinking a hundred thousand times won't reach it. the way is walking in hukam.

practice: Which pauri stayed with you: the first one, about overthinking, listening, the countless, the mint?

If you can, find it and read it slowly, the Gurmukhi sound if you can manage it, then the meaning; if you can't look it up now, say what you remember of it. Then sit with it, and let it be yours for a while.
